assertions.text: Policy thresholds (650/600 credit scores) appear in a dedicated policy column separate from applicant's actual credit score column.
assertions.evidence: Credit score threshold values (650, 600) are embedded in scenario names ('score 651 passes', 'score 650 fails') and are not shown as a separate dedicated column. There is only 'Credit Score' column with actual scores.

assertions.text: Cell values use concrete domain terms (e.g. '70', '650', 'APPROVED') — not abstract codes.
Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
assertions.evidence: First column is 'Scenario' with entries like 'Standard approval', 'Standard boundary, score 651 passes'

assertions.text: Scenario names describe conditions ('Senior at lower threshold', 'Missing income') — not outcomes ('Approved', 'Rejected').
assertions.evidence: Scenarios describe conditions: 'Standard approval', 'Standard boundary, score 651 passes', 'Senior rejection, no stable income', 'Age 64 uses standard threshold'

assertions.text: Column names use domain/business language (e.g. 'Age', 'Credit score', 'Stable income', 'Decision?') — not code identifiers.
At least one output column name ends with '?' (e.g. 'Decision?' or 'Status?')
assertions.evidence: Column 'Status?' ends with a question mark

assertions.text: Test method body contains no if or switch statements
assertions.evidence: Method body is: assertEquals(status, service.evaluateLoan(age, creditScore, stableIncome)); — no conditionals

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
assertions.evidence: @DisplayName, then @Description, then @TableTest annotations appear in correct order

assertions.text: Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title.
assertions.evidence: @DisplayName("Loan application evaluation") and method name evaluatesLoanApplication

assertions.text: If @Description is present and text is longer than one short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string), not string concatenation with +.
Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules.
assertions.evidence: Response contains only one @TableTest method mixing all concerns: age boundaries, credit thresholds, stable income, and senior vs standard applicants in one table

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns.
assertions.evidence: Single table contains 15 rows mixing age boundaries, thresholds, and income scenarios. Rows 14-15 use value set {true, false} and rows deliberately cross multiple concerns

assertions.text: Age boundary policy, credit score categorisation, and income status are separated into distinct @TableTest methods, with a method combining these for the expected verdict
assertions.evidence: Only one @TableTest method exists. No separate methods for age boundaries, credit thresholds, or income status

assertions.text: Scenario descriptions and @Description text do not include specific field values that are already visible in table.
assertions.evidence: Scenario names include specific values already in columns: 'score 651 passes', 'score 650 fails', 'Age 64', 'Age 65' appear in scenario names and also have dedicated columns

assertions.text: The standardApplicantCreditThreshold table clearly documents the effect of stable income: above-threshold + stable income = APPROVED, above-threshold + no stable income = REJECTED.
